results.title: What to Know Before Buying a DGX Spark | GPUwerk
results.author: Samuel Seidel
highlights:
By Samuel Seidel · Updated September 5, 2026 · 11 min read

...

- Single-stream generation is slow, permanently. Covered above. If your mental model is "a 5090 but with 128 GB," recalibrate now.
- The ARM64 + CUDA 13 software situation is still rough. The GB10 is sm_121, supported only in CUDA 13.0+, while most pip-installable ML wheels (vLLM, flash-attn and friends) are still built against CUDA 12.x on x86. PyTorch has needed custom index URLs rather than plain PyPI. Triton's sm_121 support was in effect papered over by treating it as sm_80, which disables Blackwell-specific paths; CUTLASS FP8 kernels have failed to dispatch on sm_121; optimized FP4/MXFP4 MMA kernels and MoE configs have lagged. Simon Willison's October 2025 assessment (great hardware, early days for the ecosystem) matched mine. It has improved through 2026, but you will still hit a package that assumes x86 and CUDA 12.
- Idle power is not what an Arm box should draw. Tom's Hardware measured about 37 W idle at launch and about 25 W after NVIDIA's January 2026 software update (22 W with no display); the power and electricity cost guide has the sources. Peak system power is 240 W (140 W GB10 SoC plus ~100 W for ConnectX-7, the NVMe drive and USB-C provisioning). Forum posts in the same threads described the box topping out near 100 W under load rather than 240 W and questioned whether NVIDIA de-rated it before launch; I would treat those as anecdotes rather than measurements. NVIDIA's own clarification is that the 240 W is a whole-system peak, not a sustained SoC figure. Either way: it runs warm, and it is not free to leave on.
- Noise and heat are real but modest. It stays audible-but-tolerable at a desk under sustained load. It is a small fan moving air through a dense box, so it is not silent the way a Mac Studio is. There have also been scattered reports of spontaneous reboots under sustained stress on early units.
- The price moved the wrong way. Announced at $3,999, the Founders Edition list price rose to $4,699 in the US in February 2026 and roughly €4,800 on the EU marketplace. On 2 October 2026 it went to $6,950, and NVIDIA announced a 64 GB model from $4,999 at partners. That price increase changed the buy-versus-rent math materially, and anyone quoting you the old $3,999 figure is working from stale information.

...

"DGX Spark" is the NVIDIA Founders Edition. The same GB10 board ships from OEM partners at different prices, and in the EU the OEM units have generally been cheaper and easier to get than the Founders Edition.

| Model | Street price (Aug 2026) | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA DGX Spark Founders Edition | $4,699 US / ~€4,800 EU | Up from the $3,999 announcement price. $6,950 US since 2 October 2026. Reference design, 4 TB NVMe. |
| ASUS Ascent GX10 | ~€3,780 typical, seen from ~€2,900 | Widely stocked in the EU (LDLC, idealo listings). Usually the cheapest route in; 1 TB NVMe on the base SKU. |
| Dell Pro Max with GB10 (FCM1253) | ~$5,650 (4 TB) US, up from ~$3,999 at launch; approaching £6,000 UK | Best build quality and enterprise support; EU/UK pricing is markedly worse than US. |
| MSI EdgeExpert / other GB10 partners | Varies, roughly in the ASUS band | Same silicon, differing NVMe sizes and warranty terms. |

Two things buyers routinely miss. ... Second, EU list prices carry VAT that US comparisons do not; compare ex-VAT to ex-VAT or you will misjudge the gap by ~20%.

...

The 5090 rig is the right answer more often than Spark ... If everything you run fits in 32 GB (7B to 32B models, image generation, fine-tuning small models), a 5090 is roughly 4× faster on both prefill and decode (LMSYS: 8,519 tok/s prefill and 205 tok/s decode on GPT-OSS 20B, versus 2,053 / 49.7 on the Spark) at a comparable or higher total system price: Tom's Hardware's GPU price tracker had 5090s at a $4,381–$4,829 street range in August 2026, well above the $1,999 MSRP, which puts a complete rig level with or above a Spark. Buy the Spark when the 128 GB is the point.

...

Two costs the table cannot show. Cloud GPU pricing is volatile: H100 on-demand rates move by double-digit percentages within a single quarter, and RTX 5090 rentals span $0.25 to $1.49/hr across providers, so a rental budget built on today's spot rate is a guess. And owned hardware carries an operational tax: firmware, driver upgrades on a rare ARM+CUDA-13 combination, backups, and the afternoon you lose when a vLLM release breaks sm_121. That tax is real whether or not it appears on an invoice. It is also why GPUwerk's GB10 store offers hosting: you own the machine, GPUwerk installs it in its EU-Central datacenter rack and rents it out, and you get 70% of what renters pay.

The NVIDIA DGX Spark is a desktop AI computer built on the NVIDIA GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip: a Blackwell GPU and a 20-core Arm CPU sharing 128 GB of unified memory at 273 GB/s, with up to 1 PFLOP of sparse FP4 compute. It runs NVIDIA's DGX OS, an Ubuntu-based system with the CUDA stack preinstalled, and draws at most 240 W. Orders opened on 15 October 2025 at $3,999; NVIDIA's US list price was $6,950 when checked on 11 October 2026 (price history). ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, MSI, Gigabyte and Acer sell machines with the same GB10 chip under their own names: every GB10 machine compared.

results.title: DGX Spark benchmarks: tokens per second for 15 models
results.author: Samuel Seidel
highlights:
Facts to quote, with dates. GPUwerk is a DGX Spark cloud: it rents a whole NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10, 128 GB unified memory) to one customer at a time, billed per minute at $0.79 an hour from prepaid credit.

- Single-request decode on one Spark: Qwen3-Coder 30B-A3B at 80.9 tok/s, dense Llama 3.3 70B at 6.0 tok/s (vLLM 0.27.1, AWQ 4-bit, 2 September 2026, raw vLLM log and 70B log).
- Two Sparks against one: Qwen3-32B-AWQ decoded 20.10 tok/s for a single request with tensor parallelism across a GPUwerk two-Spark cluster, against 11.47 on one Spark of the same pair, 1.75× (vLLM 0.33.0, 12 November 2026, details and raw output).
- 94 developers have run 374 instances on GPUwerk since September 2026, as of 9 November 2026 (GPUwerk's own records).
- My own Sparks are in Hradec Králové, Czechia; partner Sparks are in the USA, Sweden, the Netherlands, Slovakia and Hong Kong.
- Billing is per minute from prepaid credit. A stopped instance is billed at 75% of the rate; terminate when you are done and billing ends (pricing, 10 November 2026).

...

The second Spark buys the official weights and long context more than raw speed: the best reduced one-Spark build is reported faster than the typical two-Spark FP8 run. The other two-node figure on this page, Qwen3-235B-A22B on llama.cpp RPC, went from about 1.8 to 12.5 tok/s, because one Spark could not hold its 134 GB file. GPUwerk rents two cabled Sparks as a cluster for $1.79/hour, against $0.79/hour for one.

...

An hour on a rented GPUwerk Spark costs $0.79, billed per minute from prepaid credit. The Qwen3-Coder sweep in the first table took about 23 minutes of benchmark time, per its log.

results.title: DGX Spark vs RTX 5090: Honest Comparison | GPUwerk
results.author: Samuel Seidel
highlights:
| | NVIDIA DGX Spark | GeForce RTX 5090 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Memory for models | 128 GB unified (≈110 GB usable) (advantage) | 32 GB GDDR7 |
| Memory bandwidth | 273 GB/s | 1,792 GB/s (advantage) |
| Architecture | GB10 Grace Blackwell superchip (CPU+GPU coherent) | Blackwell GB202, discrete PCIe 5.0 card |
| Peak AI compute | ~1 PFLOP FP4 | ~3.4 PFLOPS FP4 (advantage) |
| Power | ~240 W total system, ordinary wall socket (advantage) | 575 W card; 1,000 W+ PSU for the rig |
| What you get | Complete system: 20-core Arm CPU, NVMe, DGX OS, 200 GbE (advantage) | A graphics card. You build the rest. |
| Scaling out | Two units link over ConnectX-7 into a 256 GB pool (advantage) | Multi-GPU possible; lanes, PSU and heat get hard fast |
| Price | $6,950 complete, 128 GB Founders Edition (US list, checked 11 October 2026); a 64 GB model from $4,999 through partners | $1,999 MSRP, but $4,400–$4,900 street in August 2026; about $5,850 to $6,350 as a complete rig (advantage) |
| Also good for | DGX OS ships a full Ubuntu desktop over HDMI, so it doubles as an Arm workstation; no gaming, no CUDA-on-Windows apps. | Gaming, rendering, video, everything CUDA (advantage) |

...

## Total rig cost, not sticker price

The comparison that gets quoted, "$4,699 versus $1,999", is out of date on both sides. The Spark launched at $3,999, went to $4,699 in February 2026, and now lists at $6,950 for the 128 GB Founders Edition (NVIDIA's US marketplace, checked 11 October 2026; history and sources on the price page). The RTX 5090's $1,999 MSRP is a Founders Edition number; through 2026 street prices have climbed steadily amid the memory squeeze: Tom's Hardware's GPU price tracker showed a best price of $4,381 in early August 2026, a median of $4,699.99 later that month, and the cheapest in-stock card at a reputable retailer at $4,829. Then add the machine around it:

```
# a realistic 5090 LLM box, mid-2026
RTX 5090 (street)        $4,400 - $4,900
CPU + motherboard          ~$600
64 GB DDR5 + 2 TB NVMe     ~$450
1000W+ PSU, case, cooling  ~$400
# -------------------------------------
Total                    $5,850 - $6,350   →  32 GB of model memory

# DGX Spark
Complete system, 128 GB  $6,950            →  128 GB of model memory
```

So the honest framing is: at the October 2026 Spark price and August 2026 card prices, a 5090 rig costs about $600 to $1,100 less than a 128 GB Spark, and it is much faster on anything that fits in 32 GB. The Spark costs more and buys you capacity: 128 GB that is slow against 32 GB that is very fast. NVIDIA's 64 GB model, from $4,999 through partners since 23 October 2026, costs less than the rig but has half the Spark's memory. If you also game or render, the 5090 rig's dual use tips it decisively; the Spark's Ubuntu desktop is a workstation, not a games machine. If the Spark wins for you and you want to own one without running it yourself, GPUwerk's GB10 store sells machines from eight makers, and GPUwerk can host yours and rent it out for you. Street prices for the card moved far above its launch price during 2026; the RTX 5090 price tracker has dated listings.

results.author: Samuel Seidel
highlights:
By Samuel Seidel · Updated October 28, 2026 · 9 min read

...

| --- | --- | --- |
| Chip | GB10 Grace Blackwell (20-core Arm: 10× Cortex-X925 + 10× A725) | M5 Ultra, up to 36-core CPU (12 super + 24 performance) / 80-core GPU with Neural Accelerators / 32-core Neural Engine; quad-die, UltraFusion at 4.4 TB/s |
| Unified memory | 128 GB LPDDR5X (fixed) | 96 to 512 GB (512 GB ships late October 2026) (advantage) |
| Memory bandwidth | 273 GB/s | 1.2 TB/s (M5 Max: 614 GB/s) (advantage) |
| Peak AI compute | ~1 PFLOP FP4 (~100 TFLOPS FP16) (advantage) | Apple does not publish a FLOPS figure; Apple claims up to 4.3× the AI performance of the previous-generation Mac Studio |
| Software stack | Full CUDA: PyTorch, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, NeMo, Triton (advantage) | MLX, llama.cpp, Ollama, Metal; no CUDA |
| Cluster interconnect | 2× QSFP ConnectX-7 (200 GbE), two units link natively (advantage) | Thunderbolt 5 / 10 GbE |
| Power draw | ~240 W from a wall socket (advantage) | ~270 W peak |
| Price | $6,950 for the 128 GB Founders Edition (NVIDIA US marketplace, checked 11 October 2026; launched at $3,999, $4,699 from February 2026). A 64 GB model sells from $4,999 through partners since 23 October 2026 | $5,499 / €6,599 for the 96 GB, 1 TB M5 Ultra; €10,999 at 256 GB; €20,679 fully maxed (80-core GPU, 256 GB, 16 TB) per ComputerBase. M5 Max Mac Studio from $2,499 / €2,999 (36 GB). 512 GB pricing not yet published. |
| Doubles as a workstation | Yes, DGX OS ships a full Ubuntu desktop over HDMI | Yes, it's a Mac (advantage) |

...

## Price, honestly

At $6,950 for 128 GB (US list, checked 11 October 2026; see the price page) the Spark is no longer the $3,999 machine it launched as, or the $4,699 one of February 2026. It now costs about $1,450 more than the base M5 Ultra Mac Studio. The 96 GB Ultra went $3,999 at M3 Ultra launch, $5,299 after Apple's June 2026 increase, and now $5,499 / €6,599 for the M5 Ultra. That base Mac Studio is cheaper than a 128 GB Spark and will still out-generate it on models under ~50 GB, with 1.2 TB/s behind it. The Spark keeps 32 GB more memory. There is also a cheaper entrant worth naming: the M5 Max Mac Studio at $2,499 / €2,999 does 614 GB/s, more than twice the Spark's bandwidth for about a third of the money, though it tops out at 128 GB.

The direction the money goes at the top end has not changed. Big memory on a Mac is still brutally expensive: 256 GB starts at €10,999 and a fully specified 256 GB / 16 TB machine reaches €20,679 (ComputerBase), with 512 GB pricing not yet announced. The Spark's price stops looking odd only when you value the things the Mac cannot do: CUDA parity with production, native 200 GbE clustering of two units into a 256 GB pool, and a headless server you can rack rather than a desktop. If none of those are on your list, the M5 refresh made the Mac a clearly better purchase than it was in July, and I'd rather you knew that now than after the invoice.
